newsitem.title: UK: Beleaguered Major relishes UK election fight.
newsitem.headline: Beleaguered Major relishes UK election fight.

text.p: His parliamentary majority has gone, his party is deeply split over Europe and he trails badly in opinion polls, but defiant Prime Minister John Major said on Sunday he was relishing Britain's looming election battle.
In his last television interview of another turbulent year, Major said he was looking forward to "direct contact" with the voters to expound his government's economic record.

"No government will ever have gone into a general election since the Second World War with the economy in such good shape, with the prospects for the future in such good order as they are at the moment," Major told GMTV.

Broken promises not to raise tax and Britain's humiliating ejection from the European exchange rate mechanism in 1992 are among the reasons, analysts say, why Major's Conservative party is getting scant credit for the economic recovery now under way.
With a general election due by May 22 at the latest, polls show the Conservatives adrift of the main opposition Labour party by more than 20 percentage points.
Major admitted that some of his government's policies had been unpopular, but he said they had been necessary for the long-term health of the economy.
"I relish the opportunity of explaining that to the British nation and setting out our plans for the future," Major said.
Conservative strategists are hoping that the economic "feelgood factor" will come to their rescue by May.
Unemployment fell below two million this week for the first time in six years, while take-home pay in the year to September rose at the fastest rate since the go-go years of the 1980s.
But Major's precarious position in parliament means he could find it hard to soldier on until May.

The 21-seat majority he won at the 1992 general election has been whittled away by defections and by-election losses, and the 323 Conservative members of the lower House of Commons are now equally matched by 323 opposition members of parliament (MPs).

The balance of power is now held by nine Ulster Unionist MPs, who papers say will send a strong signal of their intention to maximise their influence by unveiling a tactical alliance on Monday with financier Sir James Goldsmith's Referendum party.

The power of the Unionists, who want Northern Ireland to remain part of Britain, was on show last week when British fisheries minister Tony Baldry negotiated a European fishing deal that was seen as particularly good for the province.

"I think this is a government hanging on by its fingertips with no purpose other than its own survival. The public is tired of seeing them lurching from crisis to crisis, deal to deal, day to day, drfiting directionless and without leadership," Labour leader Tony Blair told the Independent on Sunday newspaper.
Labour, which has been in opposition since 1979, has promised to wage a parliamentary guerrilla war from next month to fray Conservative nerves with a raft of late-night votes.
But Major also needs to beware of possible ambushes from restless MPs in his own ranks.

One of his MPs, David Evans, threatened on Saturday to resign if the government lets his local council raise taxes to pay off debts owed to a developer. And fellow Conservative Sir John Gorst, livid over local hospital cuts, warned earlier this month that his support could not be taken for granted.

With discipline in the ruling party already stretched to breaking point by years of wrangling over Europe, Conservative strategists acknowledge they may be forced into an election before Major's preferred date of May 1. They say the favoured alternatives are March 20 and April 10.
